title: Twice as fast: how wide a bend?
hook: A car just holds a tight bend. Double its speed. How much wider must the bend be?

knows: friction between tyres and road grips
doesNotKnow: that the safe radius depends on v² / (μ g)

misconception: Twice the speed needs twice the radius.
objective: The learner can explain that grip gives a fixed sideways force, so doubling the speed needs a bend four times as wide.

claims.text: Going round a bend of radius r at speed v needs a sideways force m v² / r, and tyre grip can supply at most μ m g, so the tightest safe radius is r = v² / (μ g).
claims.source: Circular motion: centripetal force m v² / r supplied by static friction up to μ m g (any introductory mechanics text); mass cancels.

claims.text: A bend of 50 m at 54 km/h (15 m/s) just within grip means μ = 15² / (9.81 × 50) = 0.46; at 108 km/h (30 m/s) the radius must be at least 200 m, four times as wide.
Doubling the speed multiplies the tightest safe radius by 4, because it depends on the speed squared.
The model is a flat, dry bend with a fixed grip μ = 0.46 that is illustrative, not a measured road value.
claims.source: Stated on stage as a chip ('Flat dry bend, grip μ = 0.46'); μ is derived from the question's premise.

claims.text: Other speeds on the slider give tightest safe bends of 112.5 m at 81 km/h and 312.5 m at 135 km/h under the same model.
claims.source: Node: 22.5² / (0.4587 × 9.81) = 112.5 m; 37.5² / (0.4587 × 9.81) = 312.5 m. Shown on stage as the readout, not in the reveal.

recall.question: A bend is just safe at 20 m/s. At 60 m/s on the same road, the bend must be...
recall.why: The safe radius goes with speed squared: 3 × the speed means 3² = 9 × the radius.
